name: DITRA (deficiency of the IL-36 receptor antagonist)
aliases: deficiency of the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist
generalised pustular psoriasis with IL36RN mutation

reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in IL36RN, which encodes the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist
Presents with recurrent flares of generalised pustular psoriasis, often with high fever and marked systemic inflammation
Flares may be triggered by infection, pregnancy, menstruation, or withdrawal of corticosteroids
Skin shows widespread sterile pustules on erythematous, tender skin, sometimes with mucosal involvement and geographic tongue
Distinguished from ordinary plaque psoriasis by the pustular, systemic, and relapsing nature and the earlier age of onset in many cases
Managed with therapies targeting the interleukin-36 and interleukin-17/23 pathways, alongside general biologic therapy for pustular psoriasis
Acute severe flares can be life-threatening owing to fluid loss, sepsis-like inflammation, and metabolic disturbance
reference.pathophysiology: DITRA results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in IL36RN, encoding the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist. Loss of this antagonist removes the normal brake on interleukin-36 signalling, so IL-36 cytokines drive amplified activation of keratinocytes and recruitment of neutrophils. The resulting cytokine cascade, involving downstream interleukin-8, interleukin-17 and interleukin-23 pathways, produces the sterile neutrophilic pustulosis and systemic inflammation characteristic of generalised pustular psoriasis. Because IL-36 signalling is central, biologics targeting this and related axes can control disease.
additionalDifferentials: Generalised pustular psoriasis without identified mutation
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating spongiform pustules of Kogoj and neutrophilic infiltrate
Acute-phase reactants and full blood count showing neutrophil leucocytosis
Bacterial swabs and cultures of pustules to confirm sterility
Assessment of triggers including recent drug exposure and pregnancy status
Metabolic and fluid balance monitoring during severe flares
redFlags: Extensive erythroderma with high fever and haemodynamic instability
Signs of secondary infection or sepsis complicating open skin
Significant hypoalbuminaemia, hypocalcaemia, or dehydration from skin barrier loss
Flare during pregnancy threatening maternal and fetal wellbeing
reference.prognosis: The disease follows a relapsing-remitting course; individual flares can be severe or life-threatening, but targeted anti-cytokine therapy has improved control and long-term outcomes for many patients.
pitfalls: Treating a pustular flare as bacterial infection and missing the autoinflammatory diagnosis
Abruptly withdrawing systemic corticosteroids, which can precipitate a severe flare
Failing to recognise generalised pustular psoriasis as distinct from plaque psoriasis
Overlooking metabolic and fluid derangements during extensive skin involvement
management: Targeted biologic therapy against the interleukin-36 receptor (spesolimab) to abort and prevent generalised pustular psoriasis flares
Biologics directed at the interleukin-17 and interleukin-23 pathways, and conventional systemic agents such as ciclosporin, acitretin or methotrexate, for ongoing disease control
Supportive care of acute flares with fluid and electrolyte replacement, temperature regulation, skin care and analgesia
Identify and treat triggers such as infection, and avoid abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal which can precipitate flares
Monitor acute-phase reactants, full blood count and fluid balance during severe flares, culturing pustules to confirm sterility and exclude secondary infection
Multidisciplinary dermatology-led care with input for pregnancy-related and menstrual triggers
Genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive IL36RN inheritance
Escalate to inpatient or high-dependency care for severe systemic inflammation or haemodynamic instability
